items.stem: Which term is defined as "a phloem cell with perforated end walls through which sugars flow"?
items.answer: Sieve tube
items.markingKey: Sieve tube: a phloem cell with perforated end walls through which sugars flow.

items.stem: Explain how the structure of xylem vessels is related to their functions.
items.answer: Hollow dead cells with no end walls form continuous tubes for water flow; lignified walls are strong (support) and waterproof; narrow tubes help water rise.
items.markingKey: hollow / no end walls [1]; lignin strength [1]; continuous column [1] [3]

items.stem: A celery stalk is placed in water containing a red dye for several hours. Describe and explain where the dye appears when the stalk is cut across.
items.answer: Red dots appear in a ring of vascular bundles near the outside, in the xylem, because the dye is carried up with water in the xylem.
items.markingKey: ring of bundles [1]; xylem carries water/dye [1] [2]

items.stem: Which describes the position of xylem and phloem in a stem?
options: in the veins (vascular bundles) of the midrib and leaf blade: xylem towards the upper surface, phloem towards the lower surface
phloem in the centre with xylem in the epidermis
vascular bundles in a ring near the outside: phloem towards the outside, xylem towards the inside
xylem in the centre (star-shaped), phloem between the arms of the xylem
items.answer: vascular bundles in a ring near the outside: phloem towards the outside, xylem towards the inside
items.markingKey: Stem: vascular bundles in a ring near the outside: phloem towards the outside, xylem towards the inside.

items.stem: Describe the position of the xylem and phloem in a root and suggest one advantage of this arrangement.
items.answer: Xylem in the centre (star-shaped), phloem between the arms of the xylem. Advantage: resists pulling forces; anchorage.
items.markingKey: xylem position [1]; phloem position [1]; advantage [1] [3]

items.stem: Tariq placed leafy celery stalks in beakers of red dye solution at different temperatures and measured how far the dye had travelled up the xylem after 30 minutes. Results table. Temperature / °C: 5, 15, 25, 35. Distance moved by dye / mm, trial 1: 24, 47, 75, 101; trial 2: 24, 49, 73, 100; trial 3: 24, 49, 107, 100. (a) Identify the anomalous result in the table and state what should be done with it. (b) Explain the results.
items.answer: (a) Trial 3 at 25 °C (107 mm); it should be ignored when calculating the mean (or repeated). (b) Higher temperature increases the rate of evaporation from the leaves (transpiration), so water and dye are pulled up the xylem faster.
items.markingKey: (a) trial 3 at 25 °C identified [1]; ignore / repeat it [1] [2] (b) more evaporation / transpiration [1]; faster water movement in xylem [1] [2]

items.stem: In a root, where is the xylem found?
options: In the centre, often in a star shape
In a ring near the outside
items.answer: In the centre, often in a star shape
items.markingKey: Roots have central xylem (resisting pulling forces) with phloem between the arms.

items.stem: Explain why the xylem is in the centre of a root but in a ring near the outside of a stem.
items.answer: In the root the central xylem resists pulling forces and is close to the water entering from all sides; in the stem a ring gives resistance to bending by wind.
items.markingKey: root: central for pulling / anchorage [1]; stem: ring for bending [1] [2]

items.stem: Lucas placed leafy celery stalks in beakers of red dye solution at different temperatures and measured how far the dye had travelled up the xylem after 30 minutes. Results table. Temperature / °C: 5, 15, 25, 35. Distance moved by dye / mm, trial 1: 28, 57, 85, 115; trial 2: 28, 58, 86, 110; trial 3: 27, 57, 85, 111. Calculate the mean distance moved by dye at 5 °C.
Describe the position of the xylem and phloem in a leaf and suggest one advantage of this arrangement.
items.answer: In the veins (vascular bundles) of the midrib and leaf blade: xylem towards the upper surface, phloem towards the lower surface. Advantage: supplies water close to mesophyll and removes sucrose.
items.markingKey: xylem position [1]; phloem position [1]; advantage [1] [3]

items.stem: Ravi placed leafy celery stalks in beakers of red dye solution at different temperatures and measured how far the dye had travelled up the xylem after 30 minutes. Results table. Temperature / °C: 10, 15, 20, 25, 30. Distance moved by dye / mm, trial 1: 39, 56, 70, 84, 97; trial 2: 40, 56, 71, 81, 99; trial 3: 25, 54, 69, 85, 95. (a) Explain the results. (b) Suggest one way to improve this investigation.
items.answer: (a) Higher temperature increases the rate of evaporation from the leaves (transpiration), so water and dye are pulled up the xylem faster. (b) Cut all stalks to the same length with the same number of leaves.
items.markingKey: (a) more evaporation / transpiration [1]; faster water movement in xylem [1] [2] (b) Any one from: cut all stalks to the same length with the same number of leaves; use a water bath to control each temperature; repeat each test more times and calculate a mean (to improve reliability); test more values of the temperature (smaller intervals), especially near the turning point / extremes [1]

items.stem: Which term is defined as "a difference in water potential that causes water to move by osmosis"?
items.answer: Water potential gradient
items.markingKey: Water potential gradient: a difference in water potential that causes water to move by osmosis.

items.stem: Explain how water moves from the soil into a root hair cell.
items.answer: Soil water has a higher water potential than the cell sap (which contains dissolved ions and sugars), so water moves in by osmosis through the partially permeable membrane.
items.markingKey: water potential comparison [1]; osmosis through membrane [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why plants that are transplanted often wilt.
items.answer: Root hairs are damaged or torn off when the plant is dug up, reducing the surface area for water uptake, so less water is absorbed than is lost by transpiration.
items.markingKey: root hairs damaged [1]; less uptake than loss [1] [2]

items.stem: Put these in the order in which water passes through them on its way through a plant: root hair cell, xylem in the root, root cortex cells, xylem in the stem.
items.answer: root hair cell → root cortex cells → xylem in the root → xylem in the stem
items.markingKey: root hair cell → root cortex cells → xylem in the root → xylem in the stem (all correct [2]; one pair reversed [1]) [2]

items.stem: Put these in the order in which water passes through them on its way through a plant: root hair cell, root cortex cells, mesophyll cells, xylem in the leaf, xylem in the root, xylem in the stem.
items.answer: root hair cell → root cortex cells → xylem in the root → xylem in the stem → xylem in the leaf → mesophyll cells
items.markingKey: root hair cell → root cortex cells → xylem in the root → xylem in the stem → xylem in the leaf → mesophyll cells (all correct [2]; one pair reversed [1]) [2]

items.stem: Ravi waters a pot plant on a hot afternoon in Cairo. Within an hour the drooping leaves become firm again. (a) Explain how water enters the roots. (b) Describe the pathway taken by the water to reach the leaf cells.
items.answer: (a) By osmosis into root hair cells, from soil water with a higher water potential through partially permeable membranes. (b) Root hair → cortex cells → xylem of root → stem xylem → leaf xylem → mesophyll cells.
items.markingKey: (a) osmosis [1]; water potential gradient [1] [2] (b) sequence [2]

items.stem: Explain why adding a lot of fertiliser to dry soil can make plants wilt.
items.answer: The soil water becomes concentrated (lower water potential than root cells), so water leaves the root cells by osmosis instead of entering.
items.markingKey: lower water potential in soil [1]; water lost from roots [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how water moves up the xylem in the stem.
items.answer: Water evaporates from leaf mesophyll and diffuses out of stomata, creating a transpiration pull; water molecules stick together, so a continuous column is drawn up the xylem.
items.markingKey: evaporation / transpiration pull [1]; cohesion / continuous column [1] [2]

items.stem: A 1 cm length of root has 200 root hairs. Each root hair is a cylinder 0.8 mm long and 0.015 mm in diameter. Calculate the total surface area added by the root hairs (side area of cylinder = π × diameter × length).
items.answer: 7.54 mm²

items.stem: Arjun waters a pot plant on a hot afternoon in Doha. Within an hour the drooping leaves become firm again. (a) Explain how water enters the roots. (b) Describe the pathway taken by the water to reach the leaf cells. (c) Suggest why root hairs make the plant more efficient at taking up water.
items.answer: (a) By osmosis into root hair cells, from soil water with a higher water potential through partially permeable membranes. (b) Root hair → cortex cells → xylem of root → stem xylem → leaf xylem → mesophyll cells. (c) They greatly increase the surface area of the root in contact with soil water.
items.markingKey: (a) osmosis [1]; water potential gradient [1] [2] (b) sequence [2] (c) [1]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "potometer"?
options: Drooping of a plant when cells lose turgor because water loss exceeds water uptake.
The amount of water vapour in the air.
A pore in the leaf surface, controlled by guard cells, through which water vapour diffuses out.
Apparatus used to measure the rate of water uptake by a leafy shoot, which is close to the rate of transpiration.
items.answer: Apparatus used to measure the rate of water uptake by a leafy shoot, which is close to the rate of transpiration.
items.markingKey: Potometer: apparatus used to measure the rate of water uptake by a leafy shoot, which is close to the rate of transpiration.

items.stem: Explain why the rate of transpiration increases with temperature.
items.answer: Water molecules have more kinetic energy, so evaporation from mesophyll cells and diffusion of water vapour out of the stomata are faster.
items.markingKey: more kinetic energy / evaporation [1]; faster diffusion [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why transpiration is faster in bright light than in darkness.
items.answer: Stomata open in light (for photosynthesis), so more water vapour diffuses out; in darkness stomata close.
items.markingKey: stomata open in light [1]; more diffusion [1] [2]

items.stem: In a potometer the air bubble moved 36 mm in 6 minutes. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm per minute.
items.answer: 6 mm/min

items.stem: A potometer has a capillary tube of radius 0.25 mm. The bubble moved 48 mm in 3 minutes. Calculate the volume of water taken up per minute in mm³ (volume = πr² × distance).
items.answer: 3.14 mm³/min

items.stem: A potometer has a capillary tube of radius 0.25 mm. The bubble moved 45 mm in 3 minutes. Calculate the volume of water taken up per minute in mm³ (volume = πr² × distance). When a fan was switched off the bubble moved only 18 mm in the same time. Calculate the percentage decrease in the rate and explain the change.
items.answer: 2.95 mm³/min; decrease 60%; without wind, water vapour builds up around the leaf, reducing the concentration gradient, so diffusion is slower.
items.markingKey: volume = π × 0.25² × 45 = 8.8 mm³ [1]; ÷ 3 = 2.95 mm³/min [1]; (45 − 18) ÷ 45 × 100 = 60% [1]; less air movement → water vapour not removed → smaller gradient [1] [4]

items.stem: Grace used a potometer to measure the distance moved by an air bubble in 5 minutes for a leafy shoot placed at different distances from a fan. Results table. Distance from fan / m: 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 3. Distance moved by bubble / mm, trial 1: 53, 44, 35, 25, 22; trial 2: 79, 44, 34, 26, 22; trial 3: 56, 45, 35, 25, 21. (a) State two variables that should be kept constant in this investigation. (b) Describe the trend shown by the results.
items.answer: (a) Temperature; humidity. (b) As the distance from the fan increases, the distance moved by the bubble decreases: the rate of water uptake falls.
items.markingKey: (a) Any two from: temperature; humidity; light intensity; same leafy shoot [2] (b) correct overall pattern [1]; data quoted with units / turning point given [1] [2]

items.stem: Noah used a potometer to measure the distance moved by an air bubble in 5 minutes for a leafy shoot placed at different distances from a fan. Results table. Distance from fan / m: 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5. Distance moved by bubble / mm, trial 1: 52, 38, 33, 30, 26; trial 2: 51, 39, 34, 42, 27; trial 3: 53, 38, 32, 28, 26. (a) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation. (b) Calculate the mean distance moved by bubble at 1 m, ignoring any anomalous result. (c) Suggest one way to improve this investigation.
items.answer: (a) Independent: distance from fan; dependent: distance moved by bubble. (b) 38.3 mm (c) Allow the shoot to adjust for 5 minutes at each new position.
items.markingKey: (a) independent variable = distance from fan [1]; dependent variable = distance moved by bubble [1] [2] (b) (38 + 39 + 38) ÷ 3 [1] = 38.3 mm [1] [2] (c) Any one from: allow the shoot to adjust for 5 minutes at each new position; reset the bubble with the reservoir between readings; use an anemometer to measure wind speed directly; repeat each test more times and calculate a mean (to improve reliability); test more values of the distance from fan (smaller intervals), especially near the turning point / extremes [1]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "wilting"?
options: A pore in the leaf surface, controlled by guard cells, through which water vapour diffuses out.
The amount of water vapour in the air.
Drooping of a plant when cells lose turgor because water loss exceeds water uptake.
The loss of water vapour from leaves, by evaporation from mesophyll cell surfaces and diffusion out through the stomata.
items.answer: Drooping of a plant when cells lose turgor because water loss exceeds water uptake.
items.markingKey: Wilting: drooping of a plant when cells lose turgor because water loss exceeds water uptake.

items.stem: Which condition increases the rate of transpiration?
items.answer: High wind speed
items.markingKey: Wind removes water vapour, maintaining a steep diffusion gradient.

items.stem: In a potometer the air bubble moved 72 mm in 6 minutes. What is the rate of movement of the bubble?
items.answer: 12 mm/min

items.stem: Mei used a potometer to measure the distance moved by an air bubble in 5 minutes for a leafy shoot placed at different distances from a fan. Results table. Distance from fan / m: 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5. Distance moved by bubble / mm, trial 1: 44, 33, 29, 25, 22; trial 2: 44, 34, 27, 24, 22; trial 3: 44, 33, 29, 36, 22. Identify the anomalous result in the table and state what should be done with it.
items.answer: Trial 3 at 2 m (36 mm); it should be ignored when calculating the mean (or repeated).
items.markingKey: trial 3 at 2 m identified [1]; ignore / repeat it [1] [2]

items.stem: Samuel used a potometer to measure the distance moved by an air bubble in 5 minutes for a leafy shoot placed at different distances from a fan. Results table. Distance from fan / m: 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5. Distance moved by bubble / mm, trial 1: 52, 41, 33, 31, 27; trial 2: 55, 40, 20, 31, 28; trial 3: 54, 41, 35, 30, 27. (a) Suggest one way to improve this investigation. (b) State the type of graph you would draw to display these results and what you would plot on each axis.
items.answer: (a) Allow the shoot to adjust for 5 minutes at each new position. (b) A line graph: distance from fan on the x-axis and mean distance moved by bubble on the y-axis.
items.markingKey: (a) Any one from: allow the shoot to adjust for 5 minutes at each new position; reset the bubble with the reservoir between readings; use an anemometer to measure wind speed directly; repeat each test more times and calculate a mean (to improve reliability); test more values of the distance from fan (smaller intervals), especially near the turning point / extremes [1] (b) line graph (continuous independent variable) [1]; distance from fan on x-axis and distance moved by bubble on y-axis [1] [2]

items.stem: Hana used a potometer to measure the distance moved by an air bubble in 5 minutes for a leafy shoot placed at different distances from a fan. Results table. Distance from fan / m: 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5. Distance moved by bubble / mm, trial 1: 45, 35, 29, 15, 22; trial 2: 43, 33, 29, 24, 23; trial 3: 43, 34, 29, 25, 24. (a) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation. (b) Explain the results. (c) Suggest one way to improve this investigation.
items.answer: (a) Independent: distance from fan; dependent: distance moved by bubble. (b) Closer to the fan the wind speed is higher; moving air removes water vapour from around the leaves, keeping a steep concentration gradient so water vapour diffuses out of the stomata faster. (c) Allow the shoot to adjust for 5 minutes at each new position.
items.markingKey: (a) independent variable = distance from fan [1]; dependent variable = distance moved by bubble [1] [2] (b) higher wind speed [1]; water vapour removed / gradient maintained [1]; faster diffusion from stomata [1] [3] (c) Any one from: allow the shoot to adjust for 5 minutes at each new position; reset the bubble with the reservoir between readings; use an anemometer to measure wind speed directly; repeat each test more times and calculate a mean (to improve reliability); test more values of the distance from fan (smaller intervals), especially near the turning point / extremes [1]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "source"?
options: A part of a plant that uses or stores sucrose or amino acids, such as roots, fruits or growing buds.
The sugar transported in the phloem.
A small insect that feeds on phloem sap by pushing its mouthparts into a sieve tube.
A part of a plant that releases sucrose or amino acids, such as a photosynthesising leaf.
items.answer: A part of a plant that releases sucrose or amino acids, such as a photosynthesising leaf.
items.markingKey: Source: a part of a plant that releases sucrose or amino acids, such as a photosynthesising leaf.

items.stem: Explain why a part of a plant can be a source at one time of year and a sink at another.
items.answer: A storage organ such as a tuber is a sink while it stores starch in summer, but a source when it releases sucrose for new growth in spring.
items.markingKey: sink when storing [1]; source when releasing [1] [2]

items.stem: A ring of bark (including the phloem) is removed from a tree trunk. Explain why the bark just above the ring swells.
items.answer: Sucrose moving down in the phloem from the leaves cannot pass the ring, so it accumulates above it, drawing in water and causing growth / swelling.
items.markingKey: phloem removed [1]; sugars accumulate above [1] [2]

items.stem: Is a potato tuber in summer as it stores starch acting as a source or a sink?
items.answer: sink
items.markingKey: A potato tuber in summer as it stores starch: sink.

items.stem: State whether each is acting as a source or a sink, giving a reason: (i) developing seeds in a pea pod (ii) a potato tuber in summer as it stores starch (iii) a mature leaf photosynthesising in summer.
items.answer: (i) sink — uses or stores sucrose (ii) sink — uses or stores sucrose (iii) source — releases sucrose
items.markingKey: (i) sink [1]; (ii) sink [1]; (iii) source [1]; one reason linked to releasing or using / storing sucrose [1] [4]

items.stem: A farmer in Manila removes a complete ring of bark (including the phloem but not the xylem) from the branch of a fruit tree below a cluster of developing fruits. (a) Predict what would happen to the roots in the long term if a ring was removed from the main trunk. (b) Define translocation.
items.answer: (a) Roots receive no sucrose for respiration, so they die, and then the whole tree dies. (b) Movement of sucrose and amino acids in phloem from sources to sinks.
items.markingKey: (a) no sucrose to roots [1]; die [1] [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: Explain why aphids are useful to scientists studying translocation.
items.answer: Their mouthparts enter a single sieve tube; if the aphid is removed, the mouthparts can be used to collect phloem sap for analysis.
items.markingKey: feed from one sieve tube [1]; sap collected / analysed [1] [2]

items.stem: Tomás says: "Translocation only moves sugar down to the roots." Explain whether Tomás is correct.
items.answer: Translocation moves sugar from sources to sinks in any direction, e.g. up to fruits and buds.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Translocation moves sugar from sources to sinks in any direction, e.g. up to fruits and buds. [2]

items.stem: A leaf was supplied with radioactive carbon dioxide. After 6 hours, the radioactivity was found in: leaf 55%, roots 16%, developing fruits 29%. (a) Name the substance in which the radioactive carbon was transported. (b) Name the tissue it was carried in. (c) Explain why radioactivity was found in both the roots and the fruits.
items.answer: (a) sucrose (b) phloem (c) translocation carries sucrose from the source (leaf) to sinks in any direction — down to the roots and up to the fruits.
items.markingKey: (a) sucrose [1] (b) phloem [1] (c) source to sinks [1]; both directions [1] [4]

items.stem: A farmer in Bangkok removes a complete ring of bark (including the phloem but not the xylem) from the branch of a fruit tree below a cluster of developing fruits. (a) Predict the effect on the fruits above the ring, and explain. (b) Predict what would happen to the roots in the long term if a ring was removed from the main trunk. (c) Define translocation.
items.answer: (a) They may grow larger: sucrose from leaves above the ring cannot move down past it, so more is available to the fruits. (b) Roots receive no sucrose for respiration, so they die, and then the whole tree dies. (c) Movement of sucrose and amino acids in phloem from sources to sinks.
items.markingKey: (a) larger fruits [1]; sucrose cannot leave the branch [1] [2] (b) no sucrose to roots [1]; die [1] [2] (c) [2]

items.stem: Which feature of xylem vessels allows water to flow easily?
options: They are hollow with no end walls or cytoplasm
items.answer: They are hollow with no end walls or cytoplasm
items.markingKey: Dead hollow cells form continuous tubes.

items.stem: Explain why phloem must be made of living cells but xylem need not be.
items.answer: Phloem transport (translocation) needs energy and active loading at sources and sinks, so living cytoplasm is needed; water movement in xylem is passive (transpiration pull).
items.markingKey: phloem needs energy / active [1]; xylem passive [1] [2]

items.stem: Sofia placed leafy celery stalks in beakers of red dye solution at different temperatures and measured how far the dye had travelled up the xylem after 30 minutes. Results table. State two variables that should be kept constant in this investigation.
items.answer: Concentration of dye; number of leaves / size of stalk.
items.markingKey: Any two from: concentration of dye; number of leaves / size of stalk; light intensity; humidity; time in the dye [2]

(b) Suggest one way to improve this investigation.

items.stem: How does water enter root hair cells?
items.answer: By osmosis
items.markingKey: Soil water has a higher water potential than the cell sap.

items.stem: A student in Kuala Lumpur states: "Water is pumped up the xylem by the heart of the plant." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Plants have no pump; water is pulled up by transpiration (evaporation from leaves).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Plants have no pump; water is pulled up by transpiration (evaporation from leaves). [2]

items.stem: Put these in the order in which water passes through them on its way through a plant: mesophyll cells, stomata, air spaces, xylem in the leaf.
items.answer: xylem in the leaf → mesophyll cells → air spaces → stomata
items.markingKey: xylem in the leaf → mesophyll cells → air spaces → stomata (all correct [2]; one pair reversed [1]) [2]

items.stem: A 1 cm length of root has 400 root hairs. Each root hair is a cylinder 0.8 mm long and 0.01 mm in diameter. Calculate the total surface area added by the root hairs (side area of cylinder = π × diameter × length).
items.answer: 10.1 mm²

items.stem: Amara waters a pot plant on a hot afternoon in Cape Town. Within an hour the drooping leaves become firm again. (a) Explain how water enters the roots. (b) Describe the pathway taken by the water to reach the leaf cells. (c) Explain why the leaves become firm.
items.answer: (a) By osmosis into root hair cells, from soil water with a higher water potential through partially permeable membranes. (b) Root hair → cortex cells → xylem of root → stem xylem → leaf xylem → mesophyll cells. (c) Water enters leaf cells by osmosis; vacuoles swell and cells become turgid, supporting the leaf.
items.markingKey: (a) osmosis [1]; water potential gradient [1] [2] (b) sequence [2] (c) turgid [1]; support [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "transpiration"?
options: Drooping of a plant when cells lose turgor because water loss exceeds water uptake.
The loss of water vapour from leaves, by evaporation from mesophyll cell surfaces and diffusion out through the stomata.
Apparatus used to measure the rate of water uptake by a leafy shoot, which is close to the rate of transpiration.
The amount of water vapour in the air.
items.answer: The loss of water vapour from leaves, by evaporation from mesophyll cell surfaces and diffusion out through the stomata.
items.markingKey: Transpiration: the loss of water vapour from leaves, by evaporation from mesophyll cell surfaces and diffusion out through the stomata.

items.stem: Explain how wilting can help a plant survive a hot afternoon.
items.answer: Drooping leaves are less exposed to the sun and stomata may close, reducing the surface area exposed and the rate of water loss.
items.markingKey: less exposure / surface [1]; less water loss [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why removing some leaves from a cutting before planting reduces wilting.
items.answer: Fewer leaves means less surface area and fewer stomata for water loss, while the roots are too small to absorb much water.
items.markingKey: less surface / stomata [1]; balance with limited uptake [1] [2]

items.stem: Predict and explain how the rate of transpiration of a plant changes when the plant is moved into darkness.
items.answer: It decreases: stomata close.
items.markingKey: decreases [1]; stomata close [1] [2]

items.stem: Leila used a potometer to measure the distance moved by an air bubble in 5 minutes for a leafy shoot placed at different distances from a fan. Results table. Distance from fan / m: 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5. Distance moved by bubble / mm, trial 1: 47, 34, 30, 26, 24; trial 2: 28, 35, 29, 26, 24; trial 3: 45, 35, 30, 26, 24. Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: Independent: distance from fan; dependent: distance moved by bubble.
items.markingKey: independent variable = distance from fan [1]; dependent variable = distance moved by bubble [1] [2]

items.stem: Priya measured the mass lost by potted plants (with the soil surface sealed in plastic) over 24 hours at different temperatures. Results table. Temperature / °C: 10, 15, 20, 25, 30. Mass lost / g, trial 1: 7.8, 14.7, 15.2, 37.8, 53.5; trial 2: 7.8, 15.8, 25.3, 39.6, 56.4; trial 3: 7.8, 14.8, 24.9, 38.4, 55.9. (a) State two variables that should be kept constant in this investigation. (b) Calculate the mean mass lost at 20 °C, ignoring any anomalous result.
items.answer: (a) Humidity; light intensity. (b) 25.1 g
items.markingKey: (a) Any two from: humidity; light intensity; wind speed; size of plant / number of leaves; volume of water in soil at start [2] (b) (25.3 + 24.9) ÷ 2 [1] = 25.1 g [1] [2]

items.stem: Ravi says: "Translocation only moves sugar down to the roots." Explain whether Ravi is correct.
items.answer: Translocation moves sugar from sources to sinks in any direction, e.g. up to fruits and buds.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Translocation moves sugar from sources to sinks in any direction, e.g. up to fruits and buds. [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why a part of a plant can be a source at one time of year and a sink at another. (b) Explain why aphids are useful to scientists studying translocation.
items.answer: (a) A storage organ such as a tuber is a sink while it stores starch in summer, but a source when it releases sucrose for new growth in spring. (b) Their mouthparts enter a single sieve tube; if the aphid is removed, the mouthparts can be used to collect phloem sap for analysis.
items.markingKey: (a) sink when storing [1]; source when releasing [1] [2] (b) feed from one sieve tube [1]; sap collected / analysed [1] [2]

items.stem: A leaf was supplied with radioactive carbon dioxide. After 6 hours, the radioactivity was found in: leaf 47%, roots 15%, developing fruits 38%. (a) Name the substance in which the radioactive carbon was transported. (b) Name the tissue it was carried in. (c) Explain why radioactivity was found in both the roots and the fruits.
items.answer: (a) sucrose (b) phloem (c) translocation carries sucrose from the source (leaf) to sinks in any direction — down to the roots and up to the fruits.
items.markingKey: (a) sucrose [1] (b) phloem [1] (c) source to sinks [1]; both directions [1] [4]

items.stem: Compare transport in the xylem and the phloem.
items.answer: Xylem: water and mineral ions, upwards only, dead lignified hollow vessels, transpiration pull, no energy needed. Phloem: sucrose and amino acids, in both directions from sources to sinks, living sieve tubes, needs energy.
items.markingKey: substances [1]; direction [1]; cell structure [1]; mechanism / energy [1]; one similarity (both in vascular bundles) [1] [5]

items.stem: In a stem vascular bundle, where is the phloem in relation to the xylem?
items.answer: Towards the outside
items.markingKey: In dicot stems, bundles are arranged in a ring with phloem outside and xylem inside.

items.stem: A student in Kathmandu states: "Xylem vessels are living cells full of cytoplasm." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Xylem vessels are dead, hollow and lignified.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Xylem vessels are dead, hollow and lignified. [2]

items.stem: Omar placed leafy celery stalks in beakers of red dye solution at different temperatures and measured how far the dye had travelled up the xylem after 30 minutes. Results table. Temperature / °C: 10, 15, 20, 25, 30. Distance moved by dye / mm, trial 1: 39, 54, 69, 78, 93; trial 2: 41, 52, 66, 81, 97; trial 3: 38, 53, 68, 81, 92. Calculate the mean distance moved by dye at 25 °C.
items.answer: 80 mm

items.stem: Isla placed leafy celery stalks in beakers of red dye solution at different temperatures and measured how far the dye had travelled up the xylem after 30 minutes. Results table. Temperature / °C: 5, 15, 25, 35. Distance moved by dye / mm, trial 1: 29, 35, 82, 117; trial 2: 27, 55, 87, 113; trial 3: 28, 56, 83, 111. (a) Identify the anomalous result in the table and state what should be done with it. (b) Suggest one way to improve this investigation.
items.answer: (a) Trial 1 at 15 °C (35 mm); it should be ignored when calculating the mean (or repeated). (b) Cut all stalks to the same length with the same number of leaves.
items.markingKey: (a) trial 1 at 15 °C identified [1]; ignore / repeat it [1] [2] (b) Any one from: cut all stalks to the same length with the same number of leaves; use a water bath to control each temperature; repeat each test more times and calculate a mean (to improve reliability); test more values of the temperature (smaller intervals), especially near the turning point / extremes [1]

items.stem: Freya placed leafy celery stalks in beakers of red dye solution at different temperatures and measured how far the dye had travelled up the xylem after 30 minutes. Results table. Temperature / °C: 10, 15, 20, 25, 30. Distance moved by dye / mm, trial 1: 39, 50, 62, 46, 89; trial 2: 39, 51, 63, 77, 91; trial 3: 38, 52, 66, 78, 90. (a) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation. (b) Describe the trend shown by the results. (c) Suggest one way to improve this investigation.
items.answer: (a) Independent: temperature; dependent: distance moved by dye. (b) As the temperature increases, the distance moved by dye increases (from 38.67 to 90). (c) Cut all stalks to the same length with the same number of leaves.

items.stem: Which is the correct pathway of water through a plant?
options: root hair cell → phloem → mesophyll cells → xylem
xylem → root hair cell → phloem → stomata
root hair cell → root cortex cells → xylem → mesophyll cells
stomata → xylem → root hair cell → soil
items.answer: root hair cell → root cortex cells → xylem → mesophyll cells
items.markingKey: Water moves across the root to the xylem, up the stem and into leaf mesophyll.

items.stem: Daniel writes in a revision note: "Water enters root hairs by active transport." Identify the error and write a correct statement.
items.answer: Water enters by osmosis; mineral ions enter by active transport.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Water enters by osmosis; mineral ions enter by active transport. [2]

items.stem: A 1 cm length of root has 400 root hairs. Each root hair is a cylinder 0.2 mm long and 0.012 mm in diameter. Calculate the total surface area added by the root hairs (side area of cylinder = π × diameter × length).
items.answer: 3.02 mm²

items.stem: Put these in the order in which water passes through them on its way through a plant: xylem in the root, xylem in the leaf, xylem in the stem, mesophyll cells, root cortex cells, air spaces.
items.answer: root cortex cells → xylem in the root → xylem in the stem → xylem in the leaf → mesophyll cells → air spaces
items.markingKey: root cortex cells → xylem in the root → xylem in the stem → xylem in the leaf → mesophyll cells → air spaces (all correct [2]; one pair reversed [1]) [2]

items.stem: Mateo waters a pot plant on a hot afternoon in Karachi. Within an hour the drooping leaves become firm again. (a) Describe the pathway taken by the water to reach the leaf cells. (b) Explain why the leaves become firm. (c) Explain why the plant drooped earlier in the afternoon.
items.answer: (a) Root hair → cortex cells → xylem of root → stem xylem → leaf xylem → mesophyll cells. (b) Water enters leaf cells by osmosis; vacuoles swell and cells become turgid, supporting the leaf. (c) On a hot day transpiration was faster than water uptake, so cells lost water, became flaccid and the plant wilted.
items.markingKey: (a) sequence [2] (b) turgid [1]; support [1] [2] (c) loss > uptake [1]; flaccid / wilting [1] [2]

items.stem: State why a potometer must be set up with the shoot cut under water.
items.answer: To prevent air entering the xylem and breaking the water column.

items.stem: Explain why the bubble in a potometer moves more slowly when a plastic bag is placed over the shoot.
items.answer: Humidity inside the bag increases, reducing the water vapour gradient between leaf and air, so transpiration and water uptake slow.
items.markingKey: higher humidity [1]; smaller gradient / slower diffusion [1] [2]

items.stem: Yusuf writes in a revision note: "Windy weather reduces transpiration because it cools the leaves." Identify the error and write a correct statement.
items.answer: Wind increases transpiration by removing water vapour from around the leaf, keeping a steep gradient.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Wind increases transpiration by removing water vapour from around the leaf, keeping a steep gradient. [2]

items.stem: In a potometer the air bubble moved 36 mm in 5 minutes. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm per minute.
items.answer: 7.2 mm/min

items.stem: A farmer in Cairo removes a complete ring of bark (including the phloem but not the xylem) from the branch of a fruit tree below a cluster of developing fruits. (a) Explain why the leaves on the branch do not wilt. (b) Predict what would happen to the roots in the long term if a ring was removed from the main trunk.
items.answer: (a) The xylem is intact, so water still reaches the leaves. (b) Roots receive no sucrose for respiration, so they die, and then the whole tree dies.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) no sucrose to roots [1]; die [1] [2]
